\chapter{Sun, Sky, and River}
\label{ch:gu-sun-sky-river}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear and say five everyday Gujarati outdoor words, and read and write one of them.}

Five outdoor words enter meaning-first by ear, one lesson each; an oral checkpoint scores listening and speaking apart, river reaches the page with signs taught before chapter 8, and an R1 return carries the chapter-18 face words back at their fourth spacing window.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sūraj]{\gu{સૂરજ} — hear sun}

\label{lesson:GU-C29-hear-sooraj}



\begin{quote}
Say the Gujarati words for morning and for night. Now listen twice: \textbf{sūraj}. It means \textbf{sun} — the thing whose position decides whether it is \emph{savār}, \emph{bapor}, or \emph{sānj}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sūraj\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sūraj\textquotedblright{} twice, once slowly and once at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sūraj} mean? (\textbf{Sun.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/sun}{Cambridge: sun}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chandra]{\gu{ચંદ્ર} — hear moon}

\label{lesson:GU-C29-hear-chandra}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for sun. Now listen twice: \textbf{chandra}. It means \textbf{moon} — the one you see at \emph{rāt}, and listen to the \textbf{dr} at its end pushed out as one sound.
\end{quote}

\section[Practice]{Five things outdoors, by ear}

\label{lesson:GU-C29-sky-five}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the first and the last word of the chapter before any list is read to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep two scores. \textbf{Listening} goes from sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} goes from meaning to sound. A strong score in one cannot cover a miss in the other. The third row is not new material — it is the five household words of the previous chapter, returning at their second spacing window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the five names something that happens rather than something that is there? (\textbf{varsād} — the rain.)

\section[Practice]{Nadī reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C29-nadi}



\begin{quote}
Before anything is uncovered, say the Gujarati word for \textbf{river}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Uncover \textbf{\gu{નદી}} once. Three pieces, none new: \textbf{\gu{ન}} and \textbf{\gu{દ}} from chapters 1 and 2, and the \textbf{\gu{ી}} sign on the last. Notice that \textbf{\gu{ન}} carries no vowel sign at all — that is the inherent \emph{a} the very first lesson gave you for free. Name the pieces aloud in order, then read the whole word once. This is the only word of the chapter the hand is asked for; the other four stay in the ear for now, which is the gloss-first order rather than an omission.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\gu{નદી}} once. Repair one shape if it needs it; do not start a row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does the first sign of \emph{nadī} need no vowel mark? (Because a bare consonant already carries the inherent \textbf{a}.)

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/river}{Cambridge: river}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn — the distant band, the eye, ear, mouth, and nose}
You look at the \emph{ākāsh} with an \emph{āṅkh}. These four were introduced around position 110 and have not been asked for since; at this position they are more than a hundred lessons old, which is the fourth spacing window.

\subsection*{Writing — from sound, every model covered}
Record \textbf{writing} on its own; a 5/5 in listening cannot cover a miss here.

You look at the \emph{ākāsh} through a \emph{bārī}. It reached the page nine lessons ago; this is its second window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four face words carries the neuter ending? (\textbf{moḍhũ} — the nasalized \emph{-ũ}.)
